segments.say: Lesson 23. L L M Serving, Latency & Cost. A I gateways, model routing, prompt and semantic caching, batching, streaming, quantization and fallbacks.

L L M serving is running models in production fast and affordably: routing requests, caching answers, streaming output, handling failures, and (if self-hosting) using G P Us efficiently. Here is an analogy. Running a busy restaurant kitchen: prep common dishes in advance (caching), send simple orders to junior cooks and complex ones to the head chef (routing), and serve starters while the main course cooks (streaming).

Why does this matter? Cost and latency decide whether an A I feature survives in production. A standard system-design deep dive. A few key words. A I gateway: A single proxy for all L L M calls (keys, limits, logging). Semantic cache: Reuse answers to similar questions. Model routing: Send each request to the cheapest capable model. Streaming: Show tokens as they are generated. Quantization: Storing weights in fewer bits to save memory.
A production L L M gateway. All L L M traffic goes through an A I gateway (LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong, cloud gateways): one place for keys, auth, rate limits, per-team budgets, logging and retries.
Semantic cache: embed the request. If a near-identical question was answered recently (similarity above a threshold), return the cached answer: ~0 cost, ~10 ms.
Model routing: send each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. Classify complexity first, or use a cascade (try small, escalate if confidence is low).
Small models handle most traffic. Frontier models handle the hard tail. Typical savings: 50–80% of cost.
Resilience: on 429s, 5xx or timeouts use retry with exponential backoff and jitter, then fail over to another provider or region. Add a circuit breaker.
Self-hosting open-weight models with vLLM or T G I: continuous batching and PagedAttention for throughput, quantization (INT8/4-bit) for memory. Good for data residency and high steady volume.

Latency levers. Streaming: users perceive time-to-first-token, not total time. Prompt (prefix) caching: providers cache a long, stable prefix (system prompt, tools, docs) for big savings on cost and T T F T. Put static content first. Smaller / faster models and shorter outputs (max tokens, concise instructions). Parallelize independent calls (retrieval plus classification). Speculative decoding on self-hosted models.

Cost levers. Model routing / cascades; semantic plus exact caches; prompt caching. Trim context: fewer, better chunks via a reranker; summarize history. Batch A P Is for offline jobs (often ~50% cheaper). Token budgets per user or team, and dashboards on cost per feature.

Self-hosted serving concepts. Continuous batching: new requests join a running batch at every decode step, for much higher G P U utilization. PagedAttention (vLLM): manages the K V cache in pages like O S virtual memory, reducing fragmentation so more concurrent requests fit. Quantization: FP16 leads to INT8/INT4 to fit bigger models and speed things up, at a small quality cost. Throughput versus latency: bigger batches mean more tokens/sec overall but slower per user.

Say it in the interview. "I'd put a gateway in front of all model calls for auth, budgets, logging and failover, with a semantic cache and provider prompt caching for repeated prefixes. A router sends easy requests to a small model and escalates hard ones. Streaming hides latency. For steady high volume or data residency, I'd self-host an open model on vLLM with continuous batching and quantization.".

Let's compare. Streaming: perceived latency, U I complexity. Prompt / prefix caching: cost plus T T F T on long static prefixes, prefix must be identical. Semantic cache: whole calls, stale or wrong hits if threshold too loose. Model routing / cascade: cost, misroutes; needs evals. Batch A P I: ~50% cost, hours of latency. Quantization: G P U memory, speed, slight quality loss. Continuous batching: throughput, per-request latency under load.

A likely interview question: How would you cut L L M costs by 60%? A strong answer: Measure cost per feature first. Then route easy traffic to small models, add semantic and prompt caching, trim context with reranking and history summaries, cap output tokens, use batch A P Is for offline jobs, and enforce budgets at a gateway. Validate quality with evals at each step.
That's it for L L M Serving, Latency & Cost. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
